title: No beginning to find
hookLine: count your mothers with twigs, your fathers with balls of clay, and the earth runs out first (SN 15.1–2)

cards: Send off a sample of your spit, and you can get back a map of where your great-great-grandparents lived. Go back far enough, though, and the branches multiply faster than anyone can count.
Two parents, four grandparents, eight, sixteen, and soon the chart is wider than the page. The Buddha starts the chapter on the long round of lives with a family tree too.
But instead of paper, he uses all the grass in India, and then the whole earth.

teach.b: SN 15.1 opens with a sentence the rest of the chapter keeps returning to. This round of wandering, monks, is without a discoverable beginning.
No first point can be found where beings, blocked by not knowing and tied by craving, started roaming.

teach.h: GRASS AND STICKS: MY MOTHER'S MOTHER
teach.b: Suppose someone cut all the grass, sticks, branches and leaves in India, gathered them in one heap, and cut them into little sticks four fingers long.

Then, laying them down one at a time, they counted: this is my mother, this is my mother's mother. The grass and sticks of India would run out before the line of mothers did. SN 15.2 does the same with the earth.

teach.h: BALLS OF CLAY: MY FATHER'S FATHER
teach.b: Roll it into balls of clay the size of a jujube seed and lay them down: this is my father, this is my father's father. The earth runs out first.

teach.h: ANYONE MAY ONCE HAVE BEEN FAMILY
teach.b: Then the conclusion: for so long you have experienced loss and suffering. It's enough to grow weary of all this, and to be free. The images stretch the mind until it gives up looking for the edge.
Not a large number; no number at all. A little later in the same chapter, the Buddha draws out one surprising consequence.
It is hard, he says, to find a being who has not at some time been your mother, or your father, your brother, sister, son or daughter.
Some Buddhist teachers, in Tibet especially, have built a practice of kindness on that line: anyone you meet may once have been family.

how: In Tibetan Buddhism especially, students practice recognizing all beings as having once been their mothers, as a basis for compassion; teachers in other traditions draw on the same chapter of the Samyutta Nikaya.

o: with no beginning that can be found
lasting forever, with no end ahead
a family line traced back to the first

p: balls of clay from the earth

s: SN 15.1 gives a very large number of past lives
it gives no number at all: no beginning can be found.
the line of mothers outlasts all the grass of India
the grass and sticks run out first, the sutta says.
the chapter says it's hard to find a being who hasn't been your mother
some teachers build a practice of kindness on that line.

games.q: you're cutting all the grass of India into little sticks, one for each mother back through your line. what happens?
o: the line of mothers and the grass end together.
games.why: the grass runs out, and the line of mothers goes on: the round has no beginning to find.

practice: Bring to mind someone you'll see today who isn't family, a coworker, a cashier, a neighbor, someone you find difficult, and picture them clearly.
Then gently try the old thought: at some time, in some way, this one may have been my mother, my father, my brother or sister; you don't have to believe it as a fact to let it change how they look.
Notice any softening, and rest there with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Anamatagga. Without a discoverable beginning: the round of lives in SN 15, where the grass of India and the clay of the earth run out before the line of mothers and fathers. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali anamatagga: without a discoverable beginning. SN 15 is the Anamatagga Samyutta.

carryVoice: Your line: anyone may have been family. Even the person you find hardest. Six hundred fifty days now.
